This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. The authors initially formulate the problem, establish the existence and uniqueness of the stochastic solution, and then analyze a numerical discretization scheme to demonstrate its stability and convergence. The paper also compares the performance of the numerical scheme to the optimal solution by utilizing a Monte-Carlo method, establishing an a.s.-convergence result. The authors further investigate the convergence rate of the solution obtained using the Monte-Carlo method. The study is completed by examining a specific example using both numerical and analytical methods. The main achievements of this research have been previously established in theorems 2.1, 3.1, 3.2, and 4.1. The authors believe that the paper's results can be generalized to other types of stochastic control problems governed by elliptic equations. The paper is organized into four sections. The first section provides background information and formulates the problem, the second section involves the analysis of the numerical scheme, the third section examines the performance of the scheme using the Monte-Carlo method, and the fourth section presents an application of the method. Our comprehensive analysis of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. We identified a major axis that bisects the celestial sphere, which we term the "Megavoltage Axis". This axis has a signal strength of approximately 3.8σ relative to random fluctuations. We discovered a second, weaker anisotropy of 2.5σ in the Southern sky. Both anisotropies are oriented almost perpendicular to the Megavoltage Axis and are consistent with being aligned with the normal vector of the local intergalactic magnetic field as inferred by cosmic microwave background data. We also explored localized anisotropies around specific sources and found that the most prominent anisotropy is associated with the megavoltage axis but is not statistically significant. We further analyzed the distribution of highest-energy events and found that the most energetic event is concentrated near the megavoltage axis but is not statistically significant either. Both the largest-scale anisotropy and the most energetic event are oriented almost perpendicular to the normal vector of the local intergalactic magnetic field. We propose that the Megavoltage Axis may result from anisotropy in the distribution of extremely high-energy particles emitted by gamma-ray bursts during their early stages. Alternatively, it could be caused by the anisotropy of the cosmic microwave background within the local universe, modified by the integrated effect of plasma instabilities in the early universe. Both explanations are supported by the orientation of the axis with respect to the normal vector of the local intergalactic magnetic field and the megavoltage axis itself. We also suggest that the relationship between the characteristic length scales of extremely high-energy sources and the strength of the large-scale anisotropy of the cosmic-ray sky may provide a more general indicator of the distribution of these sources. We conclude that the majority of the most energetic cosmic rays detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory are likely directed towards the Megavoltage Axis, which may indicate the primary sources and the physics governing their emission. We recommend further, more sensitive observations of the Megavoltage Axis and the most energetic events associated with it to gain a deeper understanding of the physics of the most energetic cosmic rays and their sources. We also suggest that future cosmic-ray detectors be designed to detect the Megavoltage Axis and the large-scale anisotropy of the cosmic-ray sky with higher precision. A database table is considered consistent if it adheres to specified functional dependencies and contains no null values in designated rows. However, in real-world applications, databases may inadvertently incorporate erroneous data that violates these principles, leading to inconsistent tables with certain rows featuring null values and others that breach the defined functional relationships. This research aims to build upon the foundation established in [1] by introducing a hybrid inconsistency model that integrates both value-related and structural inaccuracies. In response to this new definition of inconsistency, we develop a data repair approach by creating a collection of rules that can be used in conjunction with various preference frameworks to produce preferred data repairs. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm to determine an optimal repair according to a variety of preference specifications. Notably, our solution can handle an unlimited number of data repairs, making it suitable for complex preference-based repair tasks. To illustrate the practical utility of our data repair framework, we demonstrate its application in addressing a particular issue related to data integration. Moreover, we conduct an empirical analysis to evaluate the performance and scalability of our repair algorithm using a real-world dataset. Systematic empirical evidence obtained through our experiments reveals that our algorithm excels in comparison to existing state-of-the-art repair solutions, consistently yielding superior results across a broad spectrum of preference-based repair evaluations. This achievement is particularly notable as our algorithm operates within limited memory constraints, a critical consideration in real-world applications. In addition to its individual merits, this research also aims to contribute to a broader ongoing project dedicated to developing preference-based approaches for handling inconsistencies in databases. This broader project encompasses a diverse range of research areas, including data exchange, semantic web, and data integration, among others. This study presents a count data model that combines elements of autoregressive and time-varying coefficient models to analyze and forecast data featuring non-stationary patterns. Unlike traditional Poisson AR models that assume fixed parameters across time periods, our proposed TV-PAR model allows the estimation of local time-varying parameters by employing a state space method. This approach enables us to capture changes in data dynamics over time and provides precise forecasting capabilities. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we found that the TV-PAR model generates more accurate forecasts in comparison to fixed-parameter models, especially in the presence of rapid parameter changes. Additionally, we apply the TV-PAR model to real-world data sets, comparing its performance to existing methods through metrics such as AIC, BIC, and forecasting accuracy. The results demonstrate that the TV-PAR model excels in these assessments, effectively capturing the complex temporal relationships inherent in count-based time series data. The research further highlights the TV-PAR model's capability to produce informative plots that facilitate the interpretation of dynamic patterns in data, and offers a range of software options for implementing the model. Ultimately, the TV-PAR model offers a versatile and adaptable framework for analyzing and forecasting data in various fields, including but not limited to finance, biology, and sports. The research is accompanied by freely available software, allowing for the replication of results and exploration of new applications. The R package TVPAR can be installed directly from the CRAN repository using the command "install.packages("TVPAR")". The package's documentation is accessible via the command "help(package=TVPAR)" within R. The data sets employed in the research are readily available for download at the following link: https://www.aue.edu.tw/~hschuang/download/data/TVPAR.zip. The package TVPAR is also available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/hschuang/TVPAR. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-specific coordinates. We apply this representation to automate tasks
such as object manipulation through sequential actions, without the need for an
explicit reconstruction of the object. Instead, NDFs directly predict future
points and poses by propagating a signal through a network that combines
descriptor fields, effectively treating the object as a continuous, dynamic entity.
We train NDFs using a forward model that matches the format of Neural Descriptor
Fields, obtaining promising results for both synthetic and real-world datasets. 
Real-world experiments involve manipulating objects in cluttered environments
using a single-view input, without prior knowledge of the object's pose. 
To enhance generalization, NDFs are trained to be invariant to specific action
parameters, pose, and orientation, all within the SO(3) group structure. 
We demonstrate a 3x improvement in successful manipulation attempts when compared
to a baseline model without Neural Descriptor Fields. 
Real-world experiments were conducted using a custom setup involving a Baxter
robot arm, with both small and large action commands. 
To enhance training, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called the Success
Weighted by Accumulated Distance (SWAD), which calculates the weighted distance
traveled by the predicted pose in relation to the actual pose. 
We also provide pre-trained NDF models for air-hockey and manipulation tasks.

While using photometry to measure the interstellar medium is a well-established technique, extending it to study aerosols that affect optical remote sensing in various applications presents a new challenge. By analyzing the scattering of light by aerosols in the visible spectrum, a team has developed a method to determine the optical characteristics of water droplets and soil, common types of aerosols that are easily scattered by visible light. Once the characteristics of the aerosols are known, they can be subtracted from sensed optical data to gain a clearer picture of the composition of the interstellar medium. However, removing the influence of aerosols is more complicated and requires a detailed understanding of the way light interacts with the particles, as well as accurate knowledge of the atmospheric path the light has traveled. By developing a new model that takes into account the complex patterns of light interaction and removing unnecessary data, a team has created an improved algorithm to separate the effects of aerosols and the interstellar medium from sensed optical data. This improved algorithm has been tested using actual data from a sensor and has been found to be highly accurate, reducing the margin of error to less than 0.0005 in certain cases. Once validated, this algorithm can be used in various applications that rely on optical remote sensing, such as monitoring the environment and studying the composition of distant planets. In addition, it can also be incorporated into existing satellite systems, such as the SCIAMACHY sensor on board the Envisat satellite, to gain a more accurate understanding of the interstellar medium and the composition of distant planets. In fact, a similar approach has already been successfully used with the OMI sensor on board the Aura satellite to study the composition of the Mars atmosphere during the massive dust storm that occurred in 2007. This achievement highlights the value of a interdisciplinary approach that combines expertise from physics, astronomy, and computer science to tackle complex problems in various fields. In this paper, we outline the principles of the method used to measure the interstellar medium and the characteristics of aerosols, followed by an explanation of the way light interacts with the particles in the atmosphere and the algorithm used to remove their influence. We also discuss the limitations of the current approach and suggest ways to improve it further. In conclusion, we believe that this achievement demonstrates the potential benefits of using actual measurements of the interstellar medium and the characteristics of aerosols to gain a more accurate understanding of the composition of distant planets and the composition of the interstellar medium. We present the Python library GGLasso, a tool designed to address General
Graphical Lasso computations. Originally developed to meet the analysis needs
of brain imaging data, our package offers a range of capabilities to solve a
variety of Deconvolution Algebraic problems while accommodating different
optimization methods and penalization techniques. Our implementation builds
upon the Scipy optimization framework and is compatible with both Cython and
Numpy. We believe that the versatility and adaptability of GGLasso make it a
valuable resource for researchers working with Graphical Lasso methods. The
code, accompanied by example use cases and performance assessments, is available
for public use through the GitHub platform.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been assessed for their performance. By utilizing the adjoint method, monitoring the impact of different integrators on precision and efficiency is feasible. In addition to evaluating existing methods, this study evaluates the performance of four new integrators and proposes two novel ones with adjustable accuracy. These assessments consider both the average absolute error of configurational quantities and the fluctuation of these errors over time. The study examines the tradeoffs between precision and efficiency for different optimal Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) parameters in two different integrators and shows that the optimal BCS parameter varies with time to solve different problems. The study also assesses the performance of different integrators on a molecular dynamics simulation and finds that the most precise result has the smallest average absolute error, whereas the most efficient result has the lowest average execution time. The study further investigates the impact of different integrators and simulation conditions on the performance and precision of molecular dynamics simulations and offers actionable advice to enhance their effectiveness. The development of an optimal, novel integrator called LDDM-BA that balances precision and efficiency through adjustable accuracy is also presented. The variable accuracy of this integrator is controlled by adjusting the BCS parameter, which in turn is optimized for different simulations by monitoring the average execution time and the average absolute error of configurational quantities. The performance of LDDM-BA is compared to the most precise and most efficient results obtained earlier and found to match their performance. The application of LDDM-BA to molecular dynamics simulations is also demonstrated. The code for LDDM-BA is publicly available on GitHub. The novel integrator developed in this study can balance precision and efficiency in molecular dynamics simulations by dynamically adjusting the time step based on the fluctuation of configurational quantities. The simulation code was tested on a Linux operating system and compiled using the GCC compiler. The performance of LDDM-BA was further validated by comparing the average absolute error of configurational quantities obtained using LDDM-BA to the results obtained using an exact numerical method. The average absolute error of configurational quantities decreased with an increase in the time step but at the cost of accuracy. The optimal time step for a given simulation depends on the specific problem being solved and must be determined on a case-by-case basis. The development of LDDM-BA provides a general framework for balancing precision and efficiency in molecular dynamics simulations and offers a starting point for further enhancements and improvements. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. A minimal two-dimensional lattice that exhibits a non-symmorphic wallpaper group symmetry is considered. These points can be engineered and are stable within specific momentum regions, allowing for the manipulation of their positions through applied electric field strength. This process transforms the lattice's topology, creating or closing gaps between energy levels and modifying the behavior of electrons in these areas. This advancement maintains the time-reversal symmetry of the lattice, ensuring the intrinsic purity of the Dirac points and associated electronic states. This breakthrough provides a method for creating a specific type of quantum state, known as a chiral zero-field magnetic moment, and multiple Dirac points with varying configurations, all through the application of an electric field within a lattice with precise, controllable composition. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be created via quantum-optical catalysis by using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact with the same output port, yet appear in different output ports due to the catalytic system's counter-propagating nature. We investigate the success probabilities associated with identifying these states, and explore how the catalytic system's characteristics influence these probabilities. Notably, our analysis reveals that the most distinctive feature of SPCCSs is linked to the anti-bunching effect, enabling reliable detection of these states even when the catalytic system's parameters are unknown. Furthermore, we propose a protocol for validating the catalytic system used in SPCCS generation. Overall, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between the catalytic system, the generated states, and the associated measurement outcomes. This knowledge can be applied to develop and evaluate a wide range of quantum states and systems, not just SPCCSs. Tantalum oxide, Ta$_2$O$_5$, a material with high dielectric constant and high permittivity, exhibits two stable polymorphs, Ta$_2$O$_5$-A and Ta$_2$O$_5$-B, with Ta$_2$O$_5$-B being the most prevalent form. Both ab-initio and Monte Carlo simulations suggest that Ta$_2$O$_5$ has a complex energy landscape allowing for various configurations, thereby influencing the material's electrical properties. By incorporating disorder in Monte Carlo simulations, researchers were able to replicate experimental ta values, indicating that fluctuations in local arrangements contribute significantly to the distribution of dielectric constants observed in Ta$_2$O$_5$. By introducing pinning of spontaneous polarization, researchers were able to replicate the reduced ta values associated with Ta$_2$O$_5$-B. Furthermore, simulations revealed that Ta$_2$O$_5$ can adopt a ferroelectric phase when subjected to external pressure, a property that has yet to be experimentally verified. Notably, researchers found that Ta$_2$O$_5$-B's energy state is lower than Ta$_2$O$_5$-A's due to the presence of a specific oxygen arrangement in Ta$_2$O$_5$-B, thereby explaining the stability of Ta$_2$O$_5$-B. By comparing results with available experimental data, researchers were able to validate their findings, thereby establishing a comprehensive understanding of Ta$_2$O$_5$'s ground state crystal structure. This knowledge can be utilized to tailor the material's properties and potentially create devices that rely on its unique ferroelectric and dielectric characteristics. This study also highlights the significance of considering the high-frequency dielectric response of transition metal oxides and the necessity of investigating the relationship between local arrangement, anharmonic motion, and high-frequency dielectric response. Previous research attributed the widespread dissemination of misinformation to individual-level factors such as cognitive biases and the tendency to rely on social verification. However, recent studies suggest that the role of individual-level factors has been overstated. This paper explores an alternative explanation centered on the influence of the Big Geographic Sort, a phenomenon in which people with similar socioeconomic characteristics tend to cluster in specific geographic regions, and how this clustering contributes to the widespread dissemination of misinformation. Using Reddit comments from the r/news forum, we identified and analyzed 12 prominent pieces of false information from 2019 to 2020. Our findings reveal that the likelihood of a post spreading false information on Reddit increases by 12% in regions inhabited by highly educated individuals, by 17% in regions with high median incomes, and by 15% in urban areas. These results are consistent even after accounting for individual-level factors, indicating that the Big Geographic Sort plays a significant role in facilitating the circulation of misinformation. By examining how verification behaviors vary across different geographic regions, we discovered that users in urban and high-income areas are less likely to engage in verification behaviors, which in turn contributes to the increased dissemination of misinformation in these areas. Our research highlights the significance of considering the Big Geographic Sort and the resulting clustering of verification behaviors in understanding and mitigating the spread of misinformation. By expanding the scope of potential solutions to include policy interventions aimed at modifying the social and geographic structures that facilitate misinformation dissemination, we can build on existing initiatives that primarily target individual-level factors through digital media literacy programs. Our study suggests that such initiatives may be insufficient on their own to address the problem of misinformation and that a more comprehensive approach is necessary. By providing a framework for analyzing the complex interplay between geographic, social, and online verification behaviors that contribute to the dissemination of misinformation, we hope to contribute to the development of more effective solutions for tackling this challenge. Our data and analytical methods are available for public use.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although prior studies have analyzed how humans teach others through action observation, there's a lack of understanding regarding how they use spoken language to teach others about specific tasks. This research investigates how humans combine spoken language with physical demonstrations to teach others a new skill. It identifies three distinct patterns of spoken language use in relation to demonstration: pre-demonstration, where instructions are given before the physical act; post-demonstration, where explanations are provided after the physical act; and simultaneous, where spoken language and physical action occur at the same time. These patterns are tied to the underlying structure of the task being taught and provide a framework for understanding the role of spoken language in task instruction. This work's findings have implications for developing effective teaching interfaces for robots and can be applied to related fields such as human-robot collaboration and robotics education. By integrating spoken language, robotics, and cognitive science, this research offers a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between spoken language, action, and cognitive understanding, paving the way for a more unified theory of teaching and learning. This theory can be used to design more efficient teaching methods for both humans and robots and provides a framework for studying other complex human teachings and learnings. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting and evaluating test cases. In response to this need, we present a cutting-edge, open-source test automation framework specifically designed for conversational systems. This framework provides a straightforward method for creating test scripts using a user-friendly language and incorporates a sophisticated evaluation module to guarantee that test cases adhere to the specifications of the Simplified Abstract State Machine framework. By leveraging this test automation framework, developers can effortlessly create and fine-tune test cases to pinpoint the root causes of malfunctions in their systems. We have successfully applied this framework to create test cases for a real-world ALICE chatbot ported from the CArtToSeL platform, and it has helped us identify and rectify several critical system errors. The test automation framework, available under the Apache License 2.0, can be obtained from the GitHub repository at https://github.com/alexxela/ConverseTest. By utilizing this framework, developers can create test cases for a wide range of conversational systems, and it has the potential to be integrated with existing testing tools and platforms. The accompanying technical report contains additional implementation details and a comprehensive evaluation of the testing process. The test cases developed for the ALICE chatbot have been included in the appendix. The current version of the test automation framework supports the CONVERSE protocol, but it can be easily extended to accommodate other conversation protocols by implementing the necessary listener and sender classes. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often limited by requiring a source domain with high domain similarity to the target domain or needing only basic user and item information, respectively. These constraints are frequently violated in real-world applications due to the varied and dynamic nature of user preferences. To address this challenge, a dual-target CDR method is proposed that employs a user-item interaction-based approach to capture the intricate aspects of user preferences in both domains, thereby enhancing the recommendation performance in the target domain. The proposed algorithm, MASDCR, leverages multiple feature dimensions to compensate for the lack of comprehensive information about user preferences in sparse domains and employs a hybrid strategy that combines the contribution weights of domains based on both item-specific and overall similarities. To further mitigate item-level distribution discrepancy between domains, MASDCR implements a sample-based batch hard pairwise loss function. To improve recommendation performance in data-sparse domains, MASDCR introduces an activity encouragement mechanism to encourage users and items with diverse characteristics to interact actively in the target domain. To evaluate MASDCR's effectiveness, extensive experiments are conducted on real-world datasets, revealing its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, MASDCR is demonstrated to excel in various scenarios, including single-domain recommendation, with notable improvements in recommendation accuracy. To facilitate practical implementation, the open-source code for MASDCR is made available on GitHub. With its versatility and adaptability, MASDCR is poised to tackle a wide range of cross-domain recommendation tasks and single-domain sparse data situations with enhanced performance.

Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones and seamlessly integrate with existing workflows used in optimization tasks. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on a large, previously untested dataset consisting of 2,516 scans from the ABIDE project, demonstrating that the pipeline excels at detecting severely degraded data but struggles with moderate-quality scans. By redefining the task as a multi-factorial generalization problem, we investigated the impact of various factors on the pipeline's performance and identified key distinctions between training and testing data. These distinctions include differences in brain disorders, demographic variables, and MRI acquisition protocols. We further tested the pipeline on subsets of the ABIDE dataset, distinguishing between different levels of data similarity, and found that it performs significantly better on scans with similar protocols (44.5% accurate) than on those with dissimilar protocols (14.5% accurate). These findings underscore the difficulties of developing a universally effective MRI quality control pipeline and highlight the necessity for more robust methods that can handle the inherent variability in real-world data.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation and dynamic majorization. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and yielded valuable policy insights regarding grid resilience and transportation networks. By recovering lost energy storage, our study showed that private EVs can aid in a faster grid recovery, while also highlighting the significance of prioritizing public transportation in recovery strategies to conserve precious time. Furthermore, we identified an optimal temporal pattern for private EV charging that maximizes transportation convenience while balancing demands during different recovery stages. By applying our algorithm to real-world data, we found that private EVs can recover energy more efficiently when charging is delayed until the second stage, although this may lead to increased congestion in transportation networks. Overall, our research highlights the complex interplay between energy and transportation systems and provides actionable data for policymakers seeking to enhance grid resilience and transportation convenience through targeted private EV charging strategies. By leveraging our algorithm's flexibility, future studies can explore additional factors such as grid damage costs, drive patterns, and renewable energy integration.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has been ongoing for over a decade, there's still a lack of a unified understanding of their optical characteristics and spin properties. In this paper, we review the current progress and remaining challenges of T-type damage centers in SOI materials, with a focus on Si photonic wire technology that allows for precise control over the optical properties and spin dynamics through photonic-electronic integration. Leveraging the strengths of precise control over photonic wire geometry and combination with quantum computing architectures based on electron and nuclear spins, we outline potential pathways to enhance the efficiency of optical transitions, extend the lifetimes of electron and nuclear spins, and implement efficient photon-electron spin interface through proper material engineering and design of the SOI wire structure. By overcoming the challenges and optimizing the T-type damage centers, we believe it will be possible to achieve a 50% or higher optical absorption of the strongest transition, extend the lifetimes of electron and nuclear spins to 1 second or more, and achieve a 10% or higher quantum yield of the radiative channel, which will enable reliable operation of a quantum interface based on these defect centers. With ongoing advancements in fabrication techniques, theoretical modeling, and experimental characterization, we're confident that T-type damage centers in Si photonic wire technology will serve as a robust platform for efficient quantum communication and quantum computation.

To effectively train and deploy object detectors in a variety of real-world contexts, it is crucial to evaluate their performance across diverse situations, including those with multiple categories of interest, background classes, and common distractors like occlusions and varying light conditions. Prior evaluation methods often restrict context diversity by limiting object detectors to a single class or removing background classes. In contrast, a universally applicable evaluation metric should account for the presence of background classes and other types of distractors. To address this challenge, we propose a context-aware evaluation framework that takes into consideration relevant context and effectively trains object detectors that generalize better. To demonstrate the benefits of this approach, we employ a comprehensive evaluation setup that incorporates a wide range of background classes, and our results show that it yields detectors with superior performance in real-world settings. To further showcase the versatility of our approach, we successfully adapt a pre-trained detector on a limited set of categories without significant retraining, achieving notable improvements in both accuracy and generalization. Our research and findings are applicable to a broad range of object detection tasks, including those with limited access to training data. Our code is available online for public use.

To enhance the accessibility of transplants, the ABO blood group system's restrictions have gradually been relaxed. However, type O patients, who can receive kidneys from any blood type, have a significant advantage in this scenario. We're looking to determine whether it's beneficial to prioritize type O patients over others in order to provide more compatible kidneys to a wider range of patients. We developed a mathematical model that considers various factors such as waiting time, mortality risk during waiting, the risk associated with a failed transplant, and the availability of kidney donors. By analyzing this model, we can compare the optimal policies for type O patients to those without any blood group restrictions. Our findings, obtained through numerical studies, reveal that prioritizing type O patients reduces waiting time but also increases the risk of incompatible transplants. On the other hand, not giving them priority results in longer waiting times but with a lower risk of incompatible transplants. We also explored different mortality and rejection failure rates and found that the benefits of prioritizing type O patients are more pronounced in scenarios with longer waiting lists and a higher risk of rejection failure. This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
Numerical simulations are conducted to compare the proposed solutions with an existing method. 
We also investigate the impact of key system parameters on the fair-throughput and sum-throughput values. 
In addition, we examine and contrast the OFDM-based and waveforming-based solutions in terms of throughput, power transfer efficiency, and system gain. 
Finally, we propose and evaluate two heuristic algorithms for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
Simulations show that these two heuristic algorithms yield similar results to the optimal solutions. 
We conclude by presenting an energy harvesting and storage-enabled RetTimV as an application of the SISO-OFDM system. 
This system can maximise the long-term average fair-throughput. 
We also explore and evaluate a hybrid MISO-OFDM system that employs multiple antennas during certain time bands. 
This system can provide additional gain, enhance power transfer efficiency, and increase the harvested energy. 
However, it incurs additional implementation costs. 
Therefore, we need to balance these trade-offs to achieve optimal system performance. 
This balance can be achieved by optimising the number of antennas, the time bands, and the corresponding carrier and power configurations. 
This optimisation is a non-linear high-dimensional problem that is challenging to solve. 
We propose a simple and effective solution that can balance these trade-offs and provide significant system performance gain. 
This solution works by dynamically adjusting the number of active antennas and time bands in response to changes in the harvested energy and channel conditions. 
It also enables the system to track the optimal energy storage and harvesting policy. 
We validate this solution through numerical simulations and demonstrate its effectiveness in various scenarios. 
It provides significant gain in various performance metrics, including throughput, power transfer efficiency, harvested energy, and fair-throughput. 
It is also robust and adaptable to different system configurations and channel conditions. 
It is also energy-efficient and can be applied to a wide range of energy harvesting and storage-enabled RetTimV systems.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By utilizing a level-set method to distinguish between phases and an embedded boundary technique to handle fluid-solid interfaces, we've developed a numerical approach to solve four specific problems: binary alloy solidification, Stefan problems with fluid flow, melting dendrites, and phase change with moving grid. A combination of finite element and finite difference methods is employed to solve the partial differential equations. We've tested and validated our approach against established results, demonstrating its effectiveness and accuracy. This hybrid method provides a versatile framework for simulating various solidification-melt problems and offers potential applications in fields like materials science and engineering. By leveraging this approach, researchers can explore important problems related to phase change and change of state, even in complex, dynamic scenarios. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This paper develops an initial algorithm to determine whether there exists a rationalizable Nash equilibrium (RNE) in polynomial time, with a guarantee of either identifying the existence of a rationalizable equilibrium or approximating its approximate size. Furthermore, we metamorphose this algorithm into a precise estimation method, yielding a polynomial-time estimate of the size of the rationalizable equilibrium set. Both of these algorithms operate under partial observability, learning solely about individual action payoffs. When feedback is fully observable, we devise a more sophisticated algorithm capable of precisely identifying a rationalizable equilibrium in polynomial time. To achieve these results, we introduce a novel learning setting known as the "rationalization" problem and treat it as a harder version of the standard multiagent learning problem, utilizing the solution to this harder problem to derive the aforementioned algorithms. Ultimately, our research offers an initial exploration into the rationalization problem and presents several promising future research directions. Lastly, we offer some concluding remarks and provide an outline of the paper's structure.

In complex conversations, multiple topics are often intertwined, and participants may suddenly shift to a new, unrelated subject.  Despite the prevalence of such conversations in real life, existing dialogue systems focus primarily on simple, one-topic conversations.  To address this limitation, we present a novel dialogue system that can seamlessly integrate multiple branches into a single conversation by utilizing a hierarchical structure.  Our system's design allows for effortless incorporation of new conversation branches, regardless of whether they are connected to previous discussion topics or not.  We have created a large-scale, highly-branching dialogue dataset, consisting of over 32,000 conversations with diverse topic shifts.  Our system's performance is evaluated using this dataset, and notable improvements in convergence and diversity are observed when compared to baseline models.  To further challenge our system, we have developed a series of strategically crafted dialogue scenarios that mimic real-world conversation scenarios characterized by sudden, significant topic shifts.  By leveraging these scenarios in our training regimen, significant enhancements in the system's ability to adapt to such shifts are achieved.  Our research is an important step towards creating dialogue systems that can engage in complex, multi-faceted conversations.  All system-related code and datasets are available for public use.

This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-McConnell model on the positive reals, respectively. As a result, we obtain multiple SLE driven by stochastic log-gases on the upper half-plane and the first orthant, providing a realization of the imaginary surface pairings in these domains. We also establish that the statistics of multiple SLE driven by the Dyson and Bru-McConnell models on the real line and positive reals, respectively, coincide with those driven by the stochastic log-gas model on the line and the extended positive reals, which includes the real line and the positive reals as its subdomains. Consequently, multiple SLE on the upper half-plane and the first orthant evolve in time and share the same statistics as single SLE on the extended real line evolving in time. We prove that the statistics of multiple SLE on the upper half-plane and the first orthant are equivalent to the statistics of single SLE on the line and the positive line, respectively, with the same parameter $\kappa=2$ and with the same winding measure on the unit circle. We prove that this surface shares the same conformal geometry as the upper half-plane with a branch cut along the real line. We demonstrate that the statistics of single SLE on this surface are equivalent to the statistics of multiple SLE on the upper half-plane and the first orthant, respectively. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces a novel assessment metric that combines a widely accepted conversational evaluation criterion with a measure of semantic response diversity. Specifically, it employs Natural Language Inference (NLI) to determine the semantic distinctness of generated responses. The proposed evaluation framework incorporates three individual scores: (1) a conversational relevance metric gauging how likely a generated response is to be considered relevant to the preceding conversation input; (2) a diversity NLI score calculated by determining the average semantic distinctness of each response in relation to the initial input, with higher averages indicating greater diversity; and (3) a threshold-based filtering mechanism to exclude trivial diversity. To validate the proposed evaluation framework, we conducted comprehensive experiments on both the SimpleTextForcing and Frames datasets, with the results revealing a direct correlation between diversity NLI scores and human assessments of semantic response diversity. Furthermore, the findings indicate that optimizing the proposed metric yields conversational agents that not only produce semantically distinct responses but also excel in other evaluation metrics such as BLEU and Infill. A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components. By leveraging this model, we have derived a broad, numerical representation for post-afterglow dynamics and have statistically analyzed these findings using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method. This analysis has enabled us to determine the fundamental parameters of afterglows, reconstruct the radiation spectra, and investigate various observable constraints. By simulating these observations, we have created a likelihood function that, in conjunction with the Monte Carlo code, allows us to calculate the posterior distribution of afterglow parameters. This has implications for determining afterglow properties and identifying potential shortcomings in current afterglow models. By exploring different observational scenarios, we have gained a deeper understanding of afterglow dynamics and have found that the distribution of afterglow peak frequencies is consistently narrower than previously estimated, and that the distribution of radiated energy is significantly broader than anticipated, with a peak that is more lognormally distributed than assumed. These findings have further been validated by comparing our results with existing expressions for afterglow dynamics, including narrow jet models, and with the numerical solutions for adiabatic afterglow components, from both the observer's frame and the rest frame. By incorporating the effects of magnetic fields and pair-formation lengths on afterglow dynamics, we have found that these effects become significant only at very low frequencies, and only influence the radiated energy at very low levels. Finally, we have identified the key afterglow parameters that influence the post-afterglow light curves and spectra, and have gained a deeper understanding of the various afterglow phases, including the pre-front, front, main, tail, and post-afterglow phases, and have found that only the adiabatic afterglow component exhibits a power-law light curve decay. These findings have implications for identifying the afterglow components that give rise to the observed radiation spectra and light curves in different contexts, including blazars, gamma-ray bursts, supernovae and active galactic nuclei. By investigating the interplay between the different afterglow components, we have created a comprehensive, non-linear, semi-analytical model for afterglow dynamics that has been tested against both numerical and semi-analytical solutions, and has been found to accurately reproduce the light curves and spectra of afterglows in different contexts,

Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network size and centralization levels. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. By applying percolation theory, we investigate the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, we examine the probability of a node becoming disconnected from the main component after the removal of another node that is connected to it. Based on the percolation theory, we calculate this probability for a Cayley tree network and find that it follows a power-law distribution. Furthermore, we analyze the characteristics of the nodes that lead to the disappearance of the large component and find that they are directly related to the network's parameters. This relationship enables us to calculate the average number of nodes that become isolated in a single node removal event. We also explore the distribution of these nodes and find that they are divided into two groups: one with a power-law distribution and another with an exponential distribution. This finding provides valuable insights for network immunization, as it highlights the importance of targeting specific node types that contribute significantly to network vulnerability. By applying this approach to a random graph network, we find that the distribution of the nodes that become isolated changes to an exponential distribution; however, this result requires further verification. This research offers a precise, micro-level analysis of network vulnerability, which can be applied to random graph networks and provides a foundation for future verification and validation studies. This approach to network immunization prioritizes the removal of specific node types that contribute to network vulnerability, thereby providing a more targeted and efficient strategy for reducing network vulnerability. This research provides a foundation for further studies on network immunization, particularly in random graph networks, and offers a practical solution for network administrators seeking to optimize network security by targeting specific node types. By combining theoretical models and experimental verifications, we anticipate identifying a new highly correlated Dirac metal within 4d and 5d transition metal dichalcogenides, specifically at the boundary between the strong correlation regime and marginal electron-hole coupling. This material's unique electronic properties will allow for the observation of highly correlated phenomena, such as the onset of a Mott insulating phase or Mott-Hubbard transitions, driven by external pressures or chemical doping. Furthermore, we propose that TiTe$_2$ be investigated as a promising candidate for this highly correlated Dirac scenario, leveraging available experimental data and $d$-$p$ hybridization models to accurately describe its electronic structure. By applying dynamical mean-field theory, we obtained the material's spectral and thermal properties, which are highly sensitive to the amount of electron-hole coupling and on-site repulsion. As a result, we anticipate that TiTe$_2$ can exhibit a variety of interesting phases with the application of pressure or chemical doping, ranging from a highly correlated metal to a Mott-Hubbard or an antiferromagnetic insulating phase, thus offering a rich area for further theoretical and experimental exploration.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models can be just as effective when used in a supporting role. We propose a method where a neural language model is used in conjunction with an $n$-gram model to enhance its capabilities. The $n$-gram model is used to provide initial predictions, which are then corrected by the neural model. We observe that this hybrid approach can yield significant improvements in multiple metrics, surpassing the individual performance of both $n$-gram and neural models. This method also enables the efficient deployment of small-scale neural models. Our research indicates that the optimal grammar size of $n$-gram models corresponds to the sequence length, not traditional choices like 3 or 4. Our proposed technique has been successfully applied in both unconditional text generation and related tasks like abductive summarization. Our code is available online for public use.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details. To address this challenge, we present a novel end-to-end framework called SADRNet that automatically constructs 3D faces even in the presence of substantial facial concealment. The proposed network seamlessly integrates self-alignment and dual-face regression components to ensure that the output faces are not only precise but also statistically consistent with previously trained faces. To guarantee robust performance, SADRNet is trained to be insensitive to critical facial features, and we've developed a specialized evaluation metric to assess facial reconstruction quality by considering both the quantity and quality of reconstructed features. Comprehensive experiments on several challenging datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework surpasses existing 3D face reconstruction methods in terms of both precision and robustness. Moreover, we've applied this method to create realistic facial expressions and heads for computer-generated imagery, and the resulting models are now available online. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL.

Active learning (AL) addresses this challenge by selectively training on a limited set of precisely labeled data, prioritizing images that maximally benefit from the added label information. AL's effectiveness is often evaluated using a query strategy's ability to reach the same level of performance as a fully labeled dataset, but real-world applications demand more than just matching the performance of a limited, highly expensive dataset. In this research, we examine AL's capacity to excel in real-world settings identical to those found in everyday life. To assess this, we developed a rigorous evaluation framework that compares AL to a fully labeled dataset across a range of scenarios, including different network complexity, data quality, and whether the data is used for training or evaluation. Our experiments used a robust set of metrics on a subset of the ImageNet dataset consisting of 500 classes. Our findings reveal that the most widely used AL query strategies, which prioritize images that the network is most uncertain about, do not necessarily lead to the highest level of performance when a large dataset is available. In fact, we discovered that many query AL strategies, even those that result in the selection of more diverse images, do not significantly differ from a random selection approach when evaluating the generalization to new data when the network has access to a large amount of data. Our research also explored the relationship between the size of the dataset and the effectiveness of AL, discovering that the most widely used AL query strategies are highly effective when the dataset is small but become less distinguishable from a random selection when the dataset is large. To address these findings, we developed a novel AL query strategy known as the diversity-first then uncertainty-last (DFUL) approach, which prioritizes images that are both difficult to classify and distant from the classified category. Our novel approach also highlights the importance of considering the diversity of the selected data in addition to its uncertainty in order to enhance the effectiveness of AL in real-world settings identical to those found in everyday life. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness by utilizing low-frequency conductivity measurements in conjunction with far-infrared light. By creating a $Cu/HgTe$ mesa structure with a thin barrier and conducting channels, we were able to study the transport and optical properties across the range from a single hole to highly conducting channels. Our findings show that the conductivity breakdown occurs when the hole binding energy is matched to the energy of the lowest conducting subband. This critical thickness was determined to be around $6.1 nm$ for a single-channel situation and $5.5 nm$ for a two-channel situation. By comparing the conductivity spectra with the optical absorption of a single hole, we were able to determine the effective masses of the holes within the range of $5.5 nm$ to $6.1 nm$. Our calculations revealed an interesting phenomenon where the heavy-hole mass dominates the light-hole mass when the energy of the light-hole state exceeds the energy of the hole binding energy due to the narrow well width. This effect results in a heavier effective mass than expected, which could be beneficial for high-speed electronics. By further investigating the transport properties across the range from a single hole to highly conducting channels, we were able to create a theoretical model that accurately described the conductivity spectra and optical absorption of the HgTe quantum wells. This model allowed us to determine the critical thickness where the conductivity and light absorption switch from being minimum and maximum at a specific low-frequency than any other semiconductor material. This critical thickness was found to be around $5.8 nm$ and could be adjusted by changing the composition of the HgTe alloy or incorporating impurities to achieve even thinner channels. This could potentially lead to even faster and more efficient electronics based on Dirac fermions. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning an (M/2)×(M/2) X-channelsization problem into an (M)×(M) X-matrix isolation problem. To mitigate this interference, previous research relied on static scheduling plans, assigned by base stations, which can lead to suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we developed an algorithm that allows cells to determine their own scheduling strategies in a self-interested manner, resulting in an equilibrium that maximizes the cellular association rate by approximately 13% relative to the optimal centralized solution. Moreover, our algorithm minimizes average latency and maintains a low computational complexity. To validate our solution, we conducted simulations in a scenario with 19 cells, which showed a 24% reduction in latency and a 30% increase in rate compared to the static scheduling approach. To further improve performance, we explored a modified version of our algorithm that incorporates a delay tolerance feature, enabling cells to prioritize rate or latency in a self-interested manner, resulting in a 50% reduction in latency and a 20% increase in rate in the 19-cell simulation. To evaluate our solutions in real-world scenarios, we developed a mode-scheduling policy for base stations, which can be configured using key performance indicators (KPIs), allowing for optimized cell scheduling based on varying traffic conditions. To implement this policy, we designed a mode-scheduling decision-making framework for base stations, which includes a low-computational-cost algorithm that makes self-interested scheduling decisions in a manner that maximizes the rate or minimizes the latency in a game-theoretic context, resulting in a 25% reduction in latency and a 25% increase in rate in the 19-cell simulation. In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and surpasses traditional optimization techniques for real-world datasets, as we demonstrate through comprehensive experiments. Our code is available online at this link: https://github.com/ghaleee/hamiltonian-grad-learning.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. We propose a dynamic collaborative framework that involves multiple agents and a human participant to assess the reliability of a deep learning model. The model's limited availability creates a problem, which the agents address by utilizing partially matching samples to update the model. They then assess its performance on multiple tasks using various metrics. A score indicating the model's performance is calculated, and this performance score is used to determine the model's reliability. In turn, the model's limited availability allows the agents to be rapidly trained without the need for extensive data. This training takes the form of multiple data augmentation techniques that increase the diversity of the input data, which in turn enhances the model's performance. In order to accelerate the model's convergence, we implement an adaptive learning rate for the agents' training. In addition, we introduce a mechanism to prevent the model's overfitting to the current data by gradually reducing the model's learning rate. We test our proposed framework on multiple datasets and compare its performance to existing methods. The results show significant improvements in both the accuracy and reliability of the model. In particular, we test our proposed framework on a critical application, such as traffic sign classification, using a small dataset, and the model's generalization to an analogous dataset with a large number of data samples. In this case, we find that the model's reliability exceeds 90\% after only 50 iterations. In conclusion, our proposed framework offers a flexible and dynamic approach to enhancing the reliability of deep learning models in real-world traffic scenarios. In the future, we plan to expand our proposed framework to other domains beyond transportation systems. In order to facilitate reproducibility, we make our proposed framework's source code available online. In addition, we suggest multiple avenues for future research to further improve our proposed framework. In particular, we propose integrating our proposed framework with existing active learning methods as well as other machine learning models. In addition, we propose developing a more advanced human-machine interface to enhance the model's performance even further. In order to evaluate our proposed framework's effectiveness, we conduct a driving simulation using the SUMO simulator, which demonstrates the model's ability to generalize to an analogous dataset with a large number of data samples. In this case, we find that the model's reliability exceeds 90\% after only 50 iterations. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Finally, $J_n^T$ can be distinguished from another notable invariant, the hyperbolic volume, as it is susceptible to change with virtual crossings, whereas volume is not. The construction of $J_n^T$ also yields an formula for links in a thickened torus with specific properties, and provides a new proof for the volume conjecture behavior of a specific link. The relationship between $J_n^T$ and the volume of a specific link also yields an estimate for the volume conjecture behavior of another link, and provides an inductive framework for further study of volume conjecture behavior in links. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area by applying pre-trained language models for classification tasks.  However, the limited availability of WSD datasets hinders further improvement through traditional machine learning techniques.  To compensate for this limitation, we propose an innovative Context-gloss Augmentation (CGA) framework that combines context and gloss information to enhance word sense data.  By generating synthetic context-gloss pairs, our method enriches the existing datasets, resulting in a substantial increase in dataset size.  We also introduce a novel WSD technique, Context-gloss Augmentation Network (CGAN), that leverages the augmented datasets to attain superior performance compared to baseline methods.  Experimental results on the Senseval datasets demonstrate a notable improvement in F-score measurements, with our proposed approach achieving the best scores in the BERT-based category.  Furthermore, CGAN exhibits robust performance when compared to other state-of-the-art techniques evaluated on the SemEval 2010 Task 10 dataset.  We attribute the success of our method to the effective utilization of context-gloss augmentation in augmenting existing WSD datasets, thereby enabling the attainment of superior performance in Word Sense Disambiguation.  We also provide source code for the CGAN model at https://github.com/lingua-franca/CGAN-WSD. This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. Moreover, it derives the hypergeometric representation and confirms the convergence of the integral representations by establishing the upper bound of the hyperoscidian function. It then generalizes the approach to obtain the regularized integral representation of the logarithmic derivative of the beta function. This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of generally applicable, theoretically sound, and practically effective methods for private graph machine learning. This problem is particularly pronounced in comparison to tabular data, for which a well-established body of research exists. This paper aims to provide an in-depth examination of the existing literature on DP for graph data, with a focus on theoretical formulations, graph publishing, graph learning, and GNNs, with the ultimate goal of exploring potential future research directions, identifying open problems, and highlighting areas where further investigation is necessary. This includes exploring simpler formulations, developing private attacks on graph learning, leveraging multiple layers of graph data, and integrating GNNs with other machine learning methods. This paper is intended to contribute to the advancement of the field by facilitating further innovation in differential privacy for graph-based data. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate the dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel hydrodynamic approach that applies to interacting Bose gases within a specific regime of short-wavelength fluctuations. This new method bridges the gap between previous hydrodynamic theories, which are sensitive to fluctuations, and stochastic hydrodynamic approaches, which overestimate short-wavelength corrections. Our new theory takes the form of stochastic partial differential equations that can be solved numerically and has been tested against exact results and time-evolved quantum many-body simulations. By combining this method with solutions to hydrodynamic equations, we were able to accurately simulate the spatiotemporal dynamics of interacting Bose gases throughout their entire regime of parameters. This new theory provides a powerful tool for simulating and analyzing the behavior of Bose gases in a wide range of situations, both with and without symmetry breaking, and has been applied to simulate the behavior of a Bose gas within a cavity and through a quantum point contact. Our results show that this new method accurately captures the non-equilibrium behavior of interacting Bose gases, and can be used to extract reliable quantities and dynamics from experimental and simulated data. This achievement is also a significant step towards developing a theoretical understanding of a specific phenomenon related to cold atomic gases, known as quantum shock waves. To analyze words selected at random from lengthy texts, various text samples of varying lengths were examined using large deviation theory.  These texts were derived from alphabets with correlated letter sequences, described by non-extensive Markov processes for an infinite amount of time.  The principles of large deviations were applied to obtain estimates for the logarithmic probabilities of unusual text samples.  The effectiveness of these principles was tested by generating random text based on a specific correlated letter sequence, where the associated large deviation rate function accurately captured the logarithmic probabilities of odd text samples.  Additionally, edge cases where the sequence's correlation length is infinite or the reference distribution is ergodic were also explored and showed that the associated rate functions are natural extensions of each other. We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians. Additionally, we offer a characterization of the surfaces with minimal area within a relative 1-homotopy class when the ambient space is topologically equivalent to a plane or includes a surface with a non-zero genus. In these cases, the surfaces with minimal area within a relative 1-homotopy class are homeomorphic to the original surface if it has a low enough genus, or are a subset of the surface with the same genus if it has a higher genus. This last result can also be established using a different approach that does not rely on the use of 1-homotopy groups. Finally, we offer a local version of one of these results that can be applied to surfaces with boundaries and helps to address an issue raised by an earlier study by an independent mathematician. This local version can be obtained by modifying the concept of relative 1-homotopy type and replacing it with a more basic equivalent concept that can be applied to surfaces with boundaries. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces that contain a specified set of curves as boundaries. This also enables us to investigate the relationship between these surfaces and the original surface with the same boundaries. This can be achieved by introducing a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of curves as boundaries, and investigating its properties. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights into its composition. Initial research identified a 0+1 ground state state and multiple excited 0+ and 2+ levels. However, subsequent investigations using higher-statistics data discovered a more complex picture, revealing multiple positive- and negative-parity levels lying very close in energy and displaying features of both shape coexistence and shell-gap strength. To explain these findings, an in-depth analysis of monopole tensor interactions' impact was performed, revealing their crucial role in driving the protons towards a more collectivized configuration while maintaining a small amount of spinlessness. Ultimately, 64Ni is shown to exhibit intricate features mirroring those found in heavier, more well-known examples of coexistence, and its unique structure is linked to a specific interplay between monopole tensor interactions and a relatively small amount of spinlessness. Notably, the inclusion of a 0−1 MeV neutron pair gap in the modeling is also found to accurately replicate the observed energy patterns.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment to establish their optimal parameters. However, evaluating models across various settings and selecting the ideal configuration can be computationally intensive. A common method for this task is grid search with performance evaluation via cross-validation. Yet, it yields substantial variance, hindering efficient discovery of the optimal model settings. To minimize this performance dispersion and facilitate efficient hyperparameter optimization, we propose an alternate evaluation method based on the reduction of variance in model performance assessments. We empirically evaluate this approach on multiple NLP benchmark datasets and discover that it efficiently identifies the optimal model settings with significantly reduced training time and minimal dispersion. When applied to our benchmark datasets, the reduced variance method yields comparable results to grid search, yet with approximately 500x, 100x, and 50x reduced training times for the smaller, medium, and larger sized datasets respectively. This method is particularly beneficial for large-scale NLP tasks that involve extensive training and are executed on limited computational resources. It is also suitable for machine learning model pre-training, allowing for the efficient exploration of multiple starting points with minimal training time and dispersion. This approach is readily available in the scikit-learn library under the name J-fold Cross Validation. It is, however, essential to note that this method may result in performance overfitting, albeit this risk can be mitigated by increasing the number of model initializations. This approach can be integrated into the Hyperopt optimization framework to enhance the accuracy of model performance assessments and reduce the training time and dispersion of the search process. This reduced variance method can also be used in conjunction with other optimization algorithms, such as Bayesian optimization and gradient-based optimization, to further enhance the efficiency and accuracy of hyperparameter optimization.
