Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research employs a one-way knowledge flow from the pre-trained Teacher to the Student. However, there's growing interest in exploring bidirectional knowledge learning between Teachers and Students. This survey delves into the theoretical foundations and operational aspects of Teacher-Student architectures, examining knowledge learning through parameter sharing, network design, and data utilization. It also examines the knowledge flow mechanisms, discusses the connection to related deep learning techniques, and explores applications across various knowledge learning tasks. Moreover, it highlights the challenges and potential solutions in the field. Finally, it outlines potential future research directions in bidirectional knowledge learning. By consolidating the knowledge on Teacher-Student architectures, this survey aims to provide a roadmap for further innovation in this area. Experimental verification of the discussed techniques on various knowledge learning tasks serves as an additional contribution of this survey.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata to represent functions, which enables us to solve two significant problems more efficiently: finding the most probable explanation given exact marginalisation, and constrained optimization. By converting traditional representation methods to our format, we gain several benefits: we can list all possible maximum probability explanations in polynomial time; we can determine if a particular explanation is optimal in logarithmic time; and we can find the optimal solution to constrained optimisation in polynomial time. Our approach also provides a way to convert standard representations to our format, which can be useful even in its own right. We evaluate our algorithm on a range of standard test cases and find it to be highly competitive with existing methods. By testing it on larger instances of existing problems we were able to find new boundaries and records for existing benchmarks. Our code is available online for public use. Our research also involves an interesting application to solving a particular version of the classic "misery" game theory problem.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of reduced saturation and results in the absorption of atoms at frequencies that are farther from the central beam frequency than the width of the atomic transition would suggest alone. This is analogous to an effect known as ac Stark shift, yet in this case, the primary influence is caused by the scattering of photons from the very same beam used for absorption measurements. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. By ignoring these secondary factors and focusing solely on stress as the distinguishing feature, they demonstrate that the shear thickening transition can be pinpointed at a critical stress $\sigma_c$ that marks the onset of viscosity divergence and rigidity, discovering that the resulting scaling law for viscosity holds true across a broad range of stresses, materials, and dimensions. Furthermore, by accounting for the stress required to reach asymptotic rigidity, they reinterpret the power-law behavior observed in the shear thickening regime and validate our findings using data from various experiments and simulations. These findings provide a universal understanding of the shear thickening transition, revealing that the stress at which viscosity begins to rise exponentially and the material becomes rigid is precisely the point at which the material transitions from a state of zero friction to one influenced by jamming and rigidity. This understanding has far-reaching implications for the study of non-equilibrium states, extending the concept of point junctions to non-conservative forces and revealing that shear jamming is fundamentally distinct from compressional jamming. The resulting framework also enables the accurate prediction of subsequent breakdowns in shear thickened materials, determining that the stress required to cause de-rigidity decreases in proportion to the stress deficit below rigidity, and that the resulting scaling law for viscosity during de-rigidity includes a universal exponent of three dimensions. These predictions have been validated through a range of simulations and experiments, revealing that the stress at which de-rigidity begins exhibits a second order transition with hysteresis, accompanied by oscillations in viscosity that deepen in proportion to the stress deficit. The resulting framework for interpreting viscosity during de-rigidity offers a comprehensive explanation for the widespread occurrence of material oscillations, providing a quantitative understanding of the shear thickening transition, its de-rigidity counterpart, and the distinct nature of shear jamming. The findings presented in this research have been applied to a range of problems, starting from the breakdown of concretes and mortars used in construction, through the jamming of granular materials in industrial processes and equipment, to the rupture of biological tissues and the jamming of red blood cells

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, specifically via the use of Schur Weyl duality. As a result, the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is determined for the simple Lie algebra type $A_{n-1}$. Additionally, a straightforward formula is established to calculate the (Hilbert-)Poincar\'e series for subalgebras of $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, enabling further analysis of their properties. A connection to the classical invariant theory of binary forms is also explored. A special case is examined where $n=5$, and in this instance, the Poincar\'e series of $Z_{5}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is explicitly calculated. A notable feature of this calculation is that it results in a series that coincides with the Poincar\'e series of the graded Gelfand-Tsetlin algebra when the rank is set to three. Consequently, this implies that the Gelfand-Tsetlin algebra at rank three is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{5}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, providing a significant advancement over a prior known result where only the finite-dimensional components of the algebra were found to be equivalent. A method is also developed to construct the Poincar\'e series for the finite-dimensional components of $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of basic principles of combinatorial analysis. A notable feature of this series is that it takes on a specific form that consists of a sum of distinct, ascending, monic polynomials, each corresponding to a different irreducible representation of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. A key aspect of these series is that they possess a nontrivial symmetry property related to the action of the Weyl group of type $A_{n-1}$. A connection to the theory of binary forms is also explored, providing further insight into these series. A special case is examined

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on Google's Web search engine. To investigate this, 120 participants, comprising students and working professionals, were asked to find specific definitions from a list. Half of the participants carried out the searches on a personal Google account, while the other half searched on a public account. The results showed that those searching on their personal accounts found fewer correct definitions than those on a public account. Furthermore, the difference in results was more pronounced among students than working professionals. The study also found that the most relevant information was often missed, with numbers ranging from 19 to 69% depending on the scenario. These numbers underscore the significance of Web search personalisation in work settings and highlight its potential negative consequences for individuals in positions of authority. By limiting access to information, personalisation can impede knowledge sharing and hinder the dissemination of new information and ideas. To mitigate these effects, organisations should establish clear guidelines for search engine use and provide training for their staff to help them navigate search results effectively. To further understand the impact of Web search personalisation on work settings, future research should explore how it affects specific tasks and industries. By doing so, it may also uncover new avenues for improving search engine algorithms to benefit both individuals and society as a whole. To facilitate this, a conceptual model has been developed to examine how Web search personalisation influences work settings through knowledge work on Google. This model highlights the interplay between search engine algorithms, user behaviour, work settings, and the consequences of Web search personalisation. To apply this model, future research should investigate specific work settings and search tasks to gain a more in-depth understanding of Web search personalisation's effects. To this end, a framework consisting of dimensions and indicators has been developed to guide such research. To better comprehend the intricacies of Web search personalisation's impact on work settings, future research should employ mixed-methods approaches that incorporate both qualitative and quantitative data to examine both the underlying mechanisms and statistical patterns. To facilitate knowledge sharing and future research, the findings from these case studies have been presented in the appendix. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial for treating and evaluating various abdominal and thoracic conditions. By combining data from various respiratory phases, the technique effectively reduces artifacts caused by motion, making it suitable for rapid, free-breathing scans. A numerical model simulates the signal received to determine the optimal acquisition parameters, ensuring uniform signal distribution and minimizing artifacts. The proposed method is then applied to human subjects using a numerical model and validated through in-vivo scans. The technique is also compared to and distinguished from other motion-compensated MRI sequences developed previously. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify whether observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation. This efficient exact algorithm allows for a new testing method called paired-permutation testing with clustered test statistics, which divides complex problems into simpler, more manageable sub-problems by grouping data into clusters and calculating the test statistic for each cluster independently. This approach leads to a significant reduction in the number of permutations required, resulting in an even greater speedup of 30 times for a real-world NLP task. When evaluated across a range of parameters and challenging real-world NLP tasks, our proposed method consistently outperforms the commonly used Baseline Monte Carlo approximation, demonstrating the advantages of our approach. This work is applicable to a broad range of paired-permutation testing scenarios in NLP systems. In addition to testing the statistical significance of paired data, we've also explored an analogous method called single-permutation testing, which can be used to calculate the statistical significance of individual data points. This can be particularly useful for feature importance analysis in various machine learning models. In this context, we've integrated the exact paired-permutation testing algorithm into the popular spaCy NLP library, making it easily accessible to a wide range of users. This integration enables users to easily calculate the statistical significance of individual features with just a few simple lines of code. In particular, we've provided an example code that calculates the significance of the BERT hidden layers using our exact paired-permutation testing algorithm, demonstrating the ease of use of this feature. This integration is available starting from spaCy version 3.4. This work was conducted while the first author was affiliated with the University of Colorado Boulder. The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates forcing people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning has significantly improved stock price predictions by analyzing technical and fundamental indicators. In this research, both BERT and GAN-based models are explored and compared to determine their effectiveness in predicting the IBB stock price. The BERT model was trained using a combination of technical and fundamental indicators, resulting in a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 12.01%, an Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 3.32, a Mean Squared Error (MSE) of 11.88, a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 3.44 and a Coefficient of Determination (R-squared) of 0.93 for the testing data. A Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) was also trained and produced a MAPE of 12.58%, a MAE of 3.58, a MSE of 13.19, a RMSE of 3.62 and a R-squared of 0.89 for the testing data. The stock price was predicted using a combination of both models and achieved a MAPE of 10.01%, a MAE of 2.83, a MSE of 9.01, a RMSE of 2.98 and a R-squared of 0.94 for the testing data. The use of both BERT and GAN-based models resulted in a 16.67% improvement in MAPE, a 14.75% in MAE, a 19.56% in MSE, a 14.67% in RMSE and a 0.05% in R-squared for the testing data. This research investigates the capability of future $e^+e^-$ colliders to detect beyond-Standard-Model Higgs physics using Effective Field Theories, specifically in the production of double Higgs bosons. Effective Field Theories are developed to incorporate small effects of beyond-Standard-Model physics into the Standard Model. We examined the impact of beyond-Standard-Model physics on Higgs couplings to electrons, quarks, and Higgs bosons at 1 TeV $e^+e^-$ colliders using Effective Field Theories. We considered various scenarios of new physics, including new heavy scalar or fermatic particles, and calculated the predicted signals for double Higgs production in these colliders. We found that (1) the future $e^+e^-$ colliders can detect the Standard Model prediction for double Higgs production with an integrated luminosity of 300 ab$^{-1}$, (2) the couplings of the Standard Model Higgs boson to fermions and the Higgs boson itself can be measured with high precision, and (3) the effectiveness of these colliders in searching for new physics beyond the Standard Model depends on the specific Effective Field Theory used. We also identified the most sensitive kinematic regions for detecting double Higgs production and discussed the background reduction strategies required to achieve the desired precision in measuring the Higgs self-coupling. We compared our results with similar predictions made using other codes and found they were in good agreement, except for differences in the acceptance times efficiency calculations due to the integration limits used. We demonstrated that the use of polarized electrons can significantly enhance the detection of the Higgs self-coupling, in line with previous findings. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. By estimating this drag we were able to compare it to previous research on flat plates moved through granular material. This research also highlights the importance of considering the direction of movement when studying objects similar to the cylinder used in this study. This is particularly relevant for studying sediment transport on beaches, where waves move sand grains over the surface of the beach, often pushing the grains in different directions with different forces. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Our findings were further validated by comparing our results to experimental data, utilizing a method that is insensitive to freeze-out surface's properties. Ultimately, our analysis established that the proportionality of $v_2$ and $v_3$ holds across various collisions, influenced solely by temperature and not initial geometry.

We've developed a method that uses a data-driven approach to combine biomechanical information with registration, leveraging the inherent structure of Laplace-Beltrami operators to inform the displacement field. This technique eliminates the need to solve the full elasticity problem during registration, significantly reducing computation time while achieving comparable results to state-of-the-art methods in navigation scenarios. We've tested and validated our approach using real MRI data and contrast agents, and compared it to a generic B-spline method and a model-based algorithm. Our method has been applied successfully in a clinical scenario, enabling precise identification and removal of a non-functional adrenal gland. The associated code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/pennLIDC/Vol2SurfRegistration. Our method has also been submitted to the IEEE ISBI 2021 Grand Challenge on Non-Contrast MRI Prostate Segmentation with Multi-Sequence Registration. Our code has been updated to include a new evaluation using the Grand Challenge data. The updated code is available at https://github.com/pennLIDC/Vol2SurfRegistration/tree/20210301.01. The evaluation showed that our method ranked 7th out of 34 teams in terms of Dice score and 14th in terms of 60-degree Dice score when registering multi-contrast MRI images. The updated code and results are available at https://github.com/pennLIDC/Vol2SurfRegistration/tree/20210301.01. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks such as action classification and object segmentation. Although point cloud data offers a more realistic representation of the environment, it comes with a significant computational cost for motion trajectory learning models. To address this challenge, researchers have explored self-supervised flow estimation methods, relying on metric learning techniques to link point clouds from consecutive frames based on their corresponding features. Building upon this concept, we present a novel approach that employs metric learning to differentiate the connections between point clouds from consecutive frames, relying on the distinction to infer the motion information. The proposed method consists of two primary components: a graph mixing module that blends the features of consecutive point clouds and a contrastive learning module that identifies the relationships between them. By differentiating the connections between point clouds from consecutive frames, we obtain a flow field that accurately captures the motion dynamics of the environment. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance in downstream tasks, including action classification and object segmentation, while reducing the point cloud dimensionality to a more computationally efficient cloud of 512 points. The results show that our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art self-supervised flow estimation methods while consuming significantly less computational resources. The proposed method and accompanying datasets are available online for public use. The proposed method was capable of 83.4% accuracy in action classification and 75.6% in object segmentation, both at a 20% data sampling ratio. The method's effectiveness extends to real-world scenarios, as it successfully applied to a challenging outdoor driving scene flow dataset, known for its large point cloud dimensionality, complex weather conditions, and diverse motion dynamics. The method's ability to handle large point cloud dimensionality was confirmed by demonstrating its equivalent performance to the current state-of-the-art method at a cloud size of 2048 points, but with a 5 times reduction in computational cost. The proposed method's ability to handle outdoor driving scene flow was further validated by successfully applying it to a large-scale outdoor driving dataset with multiple sequences, complex motion dynamics, and diverse weather conditions, resulting in a 2 times reduction in the bag of tricks hyperparameters. The method's capacity to handle large outdoor environments was also confirmed by successfully applying it to a dataset with a 10 times increase in the baseline distance, while maintaining a 2 times reduction in the bag of tricks hyperparameters. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops automatically identifies the system calls made by an application and compares them to previously determined baselines, enabling it to create a specific system call filtering policy for each application. This approach eliminates the need for explicit policy configuration and reduces the risk of security breaches resulting from incorrect configuration. By leveraging the existing knowledge about an application's system calls from past usage, Timeloops creates a personalized filtering policy for a limited duration, eliminating the necessity for continuous monitoring. In our evaluation, Timeloops successfully learned and applied system call filtering policies to real-world containers without any manual intervention, resulting in a 2.5 times performance improvement and a 30% reduction in eBPF overhead compared to existing static analysis techniques. Our findings also demonstrate that Timeloops can efficiently manage recurring workloads by reducing system call filtering policy recalculation time by as much as 90%. Our research includes a publicly accessible implementation of Timeloops, along with demonstration code for two widely used programming frameworks: Go and Python. By automatically generating system call filtering policies for containerized applications, Timeloops offers a practical solution for deploying production-grade, security-hardened containers. Our research is supported by funding from the National Science Foundation.

We have adapted the Probability Hypothesis Density filter to use a partially grid-based implementation of the Birth Model Density, which significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining accuracy. This modified filter demonstrates improved efficiency and comparable estimation results when compared to the original PHD filter implementation. Additionally, we showcase the potential of this method for enhanced sensor management by prioritizing measurements to match the proposed filter's limited capacity, resulting in highly comparable performance to a scenario with unlimited data. These findings are validated across various scenarios, including a challenging case with limited field-of-view sensors. This research was financially supported by the Australian Research Council.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can decide the outcome, making players' instant decisions vital. Despite individual skill levels, teamwork, and overall team strategy, a player's immediate reaction to a particular situation can either benefit or harm their team. To analyze these situations, researchers have identified several key ones, including counter-attacks, set pieces, and one-on-ones with opponents, each requiring a different course of action. By applying deep reinforcement learning to optimize these actions, a decision-making system can be created that prioritizes the maximum chance of scoring while minimizing the risk of losing the ball. To put this approach into practice, a deep reinforcement learning method is developed and tested using a simulated soccer environment, with the system learning effective actions in just 10 million simulated game moments. When applied to real soccer situations, this optimized action can lead to a 12% greater chance of scoring and a 10% lower risk of losing the ball. By extending this approach to real-world scenarios, it's possible to develop a decision-making tool for players that can enhance their performance and contribute to better game outcomes.

High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature.  This issue can be mitigated by using Ensemble FWI, which converges slowly because of its low-frequency update.  Ensemble FWI updates the model based on the spatial average of the data residuals, effectively ignoring low-frequency information.  To address this, we propose a new method called Time-Domain Extended Source Waveform Inversion (TDESWI), which applies the Ensemble FWI approach but in the time domain.  TDESWI updates the model at each time step, using the spatial average of the data residuals, and we show that this results in a better match between synthetic and actual seismic data.  By comparing it with the standard time-domain FWI, we find that TDESWI produces better results especially in areas with limited data availability.  To further enhance the method, we apply TDESWI to both pre- and post-stack data, and name it Four-Dimensional Extended Source Waveform Inversion (4DESWI), which yields the most accurate results.  We successfully apply 4DESWI to real data, obtaining highly detailed subsurface images with wide frequency content.  With the help of numerical experiments, we also determine the optimal parameters required for the time-domain and four-dimensional implementations.  Finally, we discuss the theoretical implications of time-domain and four-dimensional extensions, which could further improve the seismic imaging process.  With the development of increasingly powerful computational technology, we propose a new multi-resolution time-domain framework that can significantly reduce computational costs while maintaining high imaging accuracy.  By decomposing the time domain into multiple frequency bands, we apply different time-domain resolution scales to match the varying seismic frequency content, which enables us to achieve better imaging results with a 50\% reduction in computational costs.  We also explore other possible time-domain and four-dimensional extensions to the seismic imaging process. The surge in telework necessitated by the COVID-19 pandemic has fueled interest in
expanding experiments to a remote, hands-free operation. This work presents the
technical and software developments for freely operating an Anemometer Lab's single-point
LDV system via the Internet. The system's computer was reprogrammed using LabVIEW to
enable secure, high-speed data transfer over the network, allowing for real-time
acquisition and signal processing, including validation through measurements performed
in a controlled environment. A study on a turbulent jet was also conducted to assess
the system's performance and gather new data, with the resulting 2D velocity measurements
corroborating prior research and providing new insights into the turbulence phenomenon.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for specific applications. Our study delves into the 
feasibility of utilizing a fixed mechanical phase plate designed for high-resolution 
TEM imaging to correct spherical aberration. By combining over-collection angle 
electron solid angle distributions simulated using the TEM's multislice code, we obtained
a paraxial distribution comparable to that produced by an ideal aplanatic condenser 
system. By further adjusting the probe formation, we found it possible to achieve a 
distribution similar to that obtained with a 4C aberration corrector, both in terms 
of angular resolution and collection efficiency. Collections efficiencies of ~0.3 were 
achieved, indicating that a mechanical phase plate can be an efficient alternative 
aberration corrector in the TEM. Additionally, we examined the impact of misalignment 
on collection efficiency and found that, although it is sensitive to alignment, it can 
be minimized through precise adjustment. Notably, we discovered that a 4C corrector 
can also be approximated using a mechanical phase plate with a small amount of positive 
astigmatism, which may be beneficial for imaging sensitive samples using pre-existing 
templets. Overall, our research demonstrates the versatility of a mechanical phase 
plate and highlights its potential as a simple, fixed solution for correcting 
spherical aberration in the TEM. By tailoring the probe formation, we can achieve a 
distribution that is optimal for a specific sample, and even approximate the 4C 
corrector, thus expanding the capabilities of this affordable and straightforward 
aberration correction method.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state. Moreover, we establish sufficient conditions for both types of stability within this model. These conditions are met when the potential functions in the oscillator and the Klein-Gordon equation satisfy particular properties, which can be realized when one of the equations is linear and the other conforms to a specific anharmonic criteria. We also compare and contrast our results with existing research findings. Or else, we propose an alternative approach to achieve our results by examining the absolute value equation. Lastly, we conduct an explicit computation to illustrate our results' applicability to a particular anharmonic case.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. These conditions are directly linked to specific, detailed properties of particular subgroups associated with G, and we establish a systematic, comprehensive classification of all subgroups that satisfy the required conditions. Additionally, we identify specific relationships between these subgroups and various cyclotomic extensions of Q, building upon earlier work by Joel Thatte. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between the free generability of the ring of integers in K and a specific, well-defined subgroup of G, known as the absolute norm subgroup, which in turn is correlated with the intrinsic ramification properties inherent to the Galois extension K/Q. These findings can be viewed as an expansion upon earlier research by the same author, which focused exclusively on the Galois group A4. On the other hand, we also provide an alternative, distinct approach to determining the free generability of the ring of integers in K by utilizing the concept of G-modules over the ring of integers in a specific subfield of K, which itself is revealed to be a subfield of the rational group algebra constructed from G. Initially, we outline the theoretical underpinnings of a model that includes ALPs as an additional fundamental field with a misinterpreted outcome of a B-meson decay into two photons. We then calculate the probability of detecting these particles in various configurations of the Belle II detector. This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the KALEIDOSCOPE dataset, which assesses the linguistic knowledge of
contextualized language models across various time periods. We re-evaluate the
scores assigned to each sentence from the KALEIDOSCOPE dataset, taking into
account the semantic relationships between words and leveraging the structure of
word semantic spaces. Our analysis reveals a connection between the word's
distance from the target word and the accuracy of the contextualized model's
inference. Furthermore, we utilize this approach to investigate the phenomenon

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), comprising a central supermassive black hole surrounded by an accreting object, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic radiation. Additionally, the spins of these black holes can be determined by searching for a specific spectral feature in the electromagnetic spectrum resulting from the interaction between the electromagnetic field and the surrounding plasma. The purpose of this study focuses on the relationship between the spin of heavy AGN black holes and the mass of specific scalar, vector, and tensor fields resulting from the interaction between the fields and the black holes, specifically looking at the influence of these interactions on the spectrum of the electromagnetic radiation and comparing the derived information to empirical data on the spins of heavy AGN black holes. The analysis of the spins of these black holes was carried out using a Bayesian method and the study examined the resulting probabilities for a range of particle masses from $10^{-24}$ to $10^{-12}$ erg, along with corresponding minimum spins of the black holes, ranging from $0.02$ to $0.99$. The findings of this study are relevant to theories beyond the standard model of particle physics that propose the existence of ultralight bosons and provide constraints on their masses based on the spins of heavy AGN black holes. The derived probabilities for the masses of these bosons are also compared to the results of previous studies on the subject and the research offers a new method for determining the spins of heavy AGN black holes based solely on the analysis of electromagnetic radiation. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior satisfies specific compactness criteria, cannot be topologically characterized by a single 0-dimensional property. This conclusion holds true even when the underlying surface has just two disk components. Additionally, we find that any group of homeomorphisms for a surface with one disk component is not precompact in the topology of uniform convergence. These results build upon previous findings by M.M. Cohen and S. Moisienson. We also provide a different proof for a previously established result by Cohen. Furthermore, we explore potential connections with the surface homeomorphism group's property of having a single 0-dimensional first-order point-defect property. Alongside these results, we include a more general statement regarding the absence of a specific property that can be applied to surface homeomorphism groups. This general statement enables us to establish the absence of a particular 0-dimensional property for groups of homeomorphisms associated with compact, locally path-connected surfaces. We also examine the implications of this general statement on related topological invariants and provide a characterization of the surface homeomorphism group's 0-dimensional first-order point-defect property. This characterization can be viewed as a variant of a previous result established by the second author. We conclude by exploring potential connections between the surface homeomorphism group's 0-dimensional first-order point-defect property and the property of being topologically characterized by a single 0-dimensional property, and we propose a more general statement that could serve as a foundation for further analysis. This general statement, which we term the Surface Homeomorphism Fundamental Conjecture, has been numerically assigned the code SHFC0.1. We believe that proving this conjecture could provide valuable insights and facilitate further progress in the study of surface homeomorphism groups. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, considering two different equivalence relations on function behavior, a more advanced characterization is found to distinguish between functions that are roughly similar in behavior and those that are more fundamentally distinct, and this distinction is shown to imply a specific form of continuity for (0,1)-functions. Lastly, some notable examples of continuous functions from the literature are incorrectly identified as noncontinuous by this approach, highlighting the benefits of this proposed method.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious. Some evidence suggests a continuous, 2-part animacy spectrum, while others support a more complex, 3-segment structure comprising humans, animals, and man-made objects. We examined this issue using a novel stimulus set and functional magnetic resonance imaging. The results show that the animacy spectrum can be divided into 3 distinct regions: 1 involving human faces, 2 a mixture of animals and some objects featuring eyes, and 3 the remainder of objects. These segments are independently confirmed as separate categories by multiple subjects and exhibit distinct neural representations in the ventral temporal cortex. Furthermore, reverse correlation techniques reveal distinct patterns of stimulation associated with each segment, suggesting that the same basic neural processes underlie the representation of all objects, with additional influences related to face, eyes, or lack thereof. These findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the animacy organization in the ventral temporal cortex and its implications for theories of object perception and the origins of the human sense of self. Ultimately, this research offers a more nuanced explanation of the self-aware, it distinguishes from not-self, where the core factor is facial recognition that gives rise to self-awareness. This research also highlights the critical role of eyes in defining the category of animals and human faces and highlights the distinct neural representation of the face over the eyes. al. to incorporate "expectations" into pre- and postconditions, effectively
bridging this logic with the quantum Hoare logic introduced by Jia et al. by
treating relations as a special type of expectation with zero error. This

variables, maintaining a non-negative quantity known as "gain". Gaining a
quantity is analogous to a conditionally successful measurement in the quantum
world. Gaining a unitary program $U$ for a density operator $\rho$ is similar
to the acceptance probability of $U$ on $\rho$. In the classical case, we proved
that the reachability proof rule preserves gain, extending this result to the
quantum case required developing a method to calculate the expectation of gain

quantum relational Hoare logic is sound with respect to the relational predicate

implements an approximate unitary is given by the difference of gain
expectations. Finally, we showed that the quantum relational Hoare logic has a
sound proof system when restricted to classical programs, in this case also
obtaining an alternative derivation of the result that the reachability proof
rule preserves gain. All of our results were validated using an interactive proof
assistant named ILLICA, which is a quantum relational Hoare logic tool. In the

formula solver Z3 to handle a new type of formula that includes relations. In

gain expectations, a result that we believe is novel. In the process of

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence that can significantly influence epidemic progression. This study develops three distinct mathematical models to analyze the impact of such events on an epidemic's development. A single super-spreader event's effect on an already widespread epidemic appears to be minimal, but when applied to an emerging epidemic, it can either accelerate or slow down the epidemic's progression, sometimes even leading to the epidemic's decline. This study also examines various intervention strategies, revealing that controlling super-spreader events can be crucial in managing an emerging epidemic, but has a limited impact on already widespread epidemics. This research's mathematical findings are also representative of general renewal processes and can be applied to model epidemics in populations with periodic gatherings, revealing that super-spreader events at these gatherings can drive an epidemic forward even after it has otherwise run its course. This study's numerical methods can be easily applied to different population models and provide valuable insights into the critical role that super-spreader events play in shaping an epidemic's trajectory. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. A novel complex-valued neural network, designed to minimize the determinant's magnitude while efficiently approximating the original distribution, is introduced in this study. By training the network in small imaginary time steps, we successfully applied this method to simulate the Hubbard model at finite temperatures and temperatures that incur a severe sign problem, achieving accurate results and efficiently mitigating the sign problem. Compared to other mitigation strategies, this neural network approach demonstrates substantial advantages, as evident from our simulations of the Hubbard model. This novel neural network's potential extends far beyond the Hubbard model, enabling the treatment of any Monte Carlo sign problem. To facilitate practical applications, the code developed in this research is made publicly available. By treating the determinant of the Jacobian as a trainable parameter, we explored an alternative strategy and found it to be less effective in addressing the sign problem. The simulation data, along with the code, can be accessed via the Hubbard Model Monte Carlo Codes Repository established specifically for this purpose. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
To mimic this ability in models, we will create an unsupervised cross-task generalization framework using retrieval augmentation.
First, we train separate models for two tasks, then we use a query set from the second task to retrieve augmented data from the first task.
We use this augmented data to fine-tune the model on the first task, enabling it to excel on the second task without direct training.
Our approach yields outstanding results in both image and language processing, surpassing the performance of models trained on individual tasks or conventional unsupervised multi-task methods.

The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code is user-friendly, customizable, and compatible with various deep learning frameworks. The findings and code developed here are valuable assets for practitioners and researchers working with private deep learning. The code has been successfully utilized to achieve reduced error rates of up to 98% in tasks like image classification. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a union of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this union. Additionally, we explore connections between these boolean complexes and the poset of Peisker's $\gamma$-sets, demonstrating that its order complex shares the same homotopy type as the boolean complex of involutions. Finally, we offer a specific case study involving the boolean complex of involutions for the Fock space over the root system A_n. As a result, we obtain the homotopy type of the order complex of Peisker's $\gamma$-sets for the A_n type, as well as a formula counting the number of spheres within this union, which can also be interpreted as the number of non-isomorphic, irreducible, monodromic modules for the quantum group U_q(A_n). As an important side note, we correct an earlier formula proposed by Kirillov and Nakanishi.

We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine the distribution of 34,410 stars analyzed by the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Evolution Spectroscopy (APOGEE) project. By utilizing a two-component model to account for vertical gradients and comparing actual measurements to predicted values, we identified patterns in abundance discrepancies from expected values. Notable features include a positive correlation between [NeII]/[FeII] and [C/N], likely resulting from chemical variations induced by whole-disc stellar mass. We determined the standard error of the fit to be approximately 4.4 x 10 to the power of negative 2.  We also discovered a linear relation between [Mg/N] and [C/N], which may arise from a similar mass-related effect. Furthermore, we found a more significant positive [C/N] gradient near the Galactic center than near the Galactic center, which could be explained by a combination of mass-related effects and bulge formation. A linear model was insufficient to accurately represent [Al/N] and [O/N] variations, suggesting additional influencing factors beyond the examined parameters. We determined the standard error of the fit to be approximately 6.5 x 10 to the power of negative 2  for these two elements. We also observed a range of [C/N], likely resulting from different metallicity and mass-related processes, which could be interpreted as evidence for both disc and bulge populations. We analyzed residual abundance distributions by dividing the data set into multiple metallicity groups and found a linear relation between [C/N], defined as (C is less than N)/ (C is plus N), and metallicity, which could be explained by the contribution of both low-mass main-sequence stars and asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars. We estimated the standard error of the fit to be approximately 0.012. We also determined the error of the fit for the oxygen isotope ratio distribution to be approximately 0.015. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused significant disruptions to society, economy and politics.  In this environment, online medical rumors rapidly spread across China, posing a substantial threat to public health, infrastructure and governance.  To address this pressing issue, the Chinese government launched a nationwide effort to combat medical misinformation.  Despite these efforts, medical rumors continued to circulate and evolve.  To better understand this phenomenon, we collected 4,866 real-time posts containing medical rumors from Chinese social media platforms Weibo and Baidu Zhidao from January 2020 to March 2020.  By developing a machine learning-based approach to identify and categorize medical rumors, we distinguished 2,514 posts as authentic medical rumors from 2,352 spam posts and 1,000 posts with other contents.  In examining the influence of medical rumors, we employed the spreading influence prediction model to calculate the expected spreading influence of each rumor and discovered that only 12.1% of medical rumors were likely to spread widely.  Furthermore, through statistical analysis, we found that medical rumors that spread extensively often featured concrete false evidence, emphasized severe consequences, emphasized government cover-ups, and targeted specific, rather than broad, populations.  To gauge the rate at which medical rumors spread, we calculated an average spreading speed of 0.104 new followers per minute.  By modeling the dynamics of rumor propagation, we determined that medical rumors often adopted a rapid initial growth phase, followed by a slower decline.  In exploring potential factors influencing the spread of medical rumors, we discovered that those targeting older adults (65 and above) proved more likely to spread extensively.  In addition, we found that medical rumors circulating during the initial COVID-19 outbreak period (January 2020) were more likely to spread widely than those emerging in subsequent periods.  Finally, to assess the impact of medical rumors on public behavior during the COVID-19 pandemic, we conducted a survey among 1,000 Chinese adults and found that approximately 43% reported changing their behavior in response to medical misinformation, with the majority adopting preventive measures such as wearing a mask, maintaining social distancing, or engaging in enhanced personal hygiene.  In conclusion, our research into the dynamics of medical rumor propagation during the COVID-19 pandemic reveals the critical role played by older adult targets and initial growth phase characteristics in determining a rumor's spread and influence. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae. By utilizing the H-alpha and [NII] lines' ratios, a technique called semi-empirical calibration can determine this distance. This method was put to the test on galaxies located within the Fornax cluster, a well-studied nearby galaxy cluster that has been explored in great detail. A study of the H-alpha and [NII] lines emitted by planetary nebulae within three galaxies revealed their respective distances. These measurements were then compared to previously established distance estimates derived from other methods. A study of 1440 detected planetary nebulae in three galaxies, with luminosities ranging 10^38 to 10^40 erg/s, showed their distances to be 19.86 megaparsecs with a 0.04 megaparsec margin of error. This finding is consistent with previous measurements obtained using other methods. Furthermore, it was determined that the Planetary Nebulae Density Profile exhibits a 6 megaparsec inverse radius. This information can be utilized to calculate the total planetary nebulae luminosity within a galaxy, and with the semi-empirical calibration technique, determine its distance. This approach has the added benefit of providing a precise measurement of the Planetary Nebulae Density Profile slope, with a 0.2 margin of error, and valuable insights into the galactic parameters such as mass and star formation rate. This method has the potential to accurately measure the distance to a wide range of galaxies with a minimal error margin. With the aid of a state-of-the-art H-alpha survey of the Fornax cluster, a detailed and reliable distance map to the galaxies within the cluster has been created. This information can also be utilized to derive a precise estimate of the Planetary Nebulae Density Profile and the distribution of Planetary Nebulae luminosities within the galaxies. This is particularly useful for gaining a better understanding of the formation and evolution of the galaxies and the distribution of their central regions. This new approach and the resulting distance measurements to the galaxies within the Fornax cluster can be found in a comprehensive database that is readily available for further scientific analysis. This research is part of the comprehensive Fornax3D project, a large-scale H-alpha survey of the galaxies within the Fornax cluster that has yielded a vast amount of data on the formation and evolution of galaxies. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an increasing need to analyze these data efficiently. Analyzing these data enables healthcare professionals to prevent medical crises, among other benefits. Although recent advancements in artificial intelligence have produced accurate prediction models, implementing an effective real-time streaming system to support continuous data analysis poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, a high-performance streaming engine called LifeStream has been developed, capable of efficiently processing periodic streams in a single node. LifeStream achieves this by utilizing a hybrid approach that combines batch and incremental processing methods. As a result, LifeStream outperforms other streaming engines and enables real-time execution of complex prediction tasks on large datasets. To further increase scalability, LifeStream was modified to support distributed processing, resulting in a 13x improvement in processing time when moving from a single node to a four-node cluster. The LifeStream engine has been implemented and tested using real-world data from a university hospital, leading to accurate predictions with an F1-score of 0.95. The LifeStream engine has been made available open-source, enabling users to download and utilize it for their own purposes. The development of LifeStream highlights the potential for efficient real-time analysis of patient data, paving the way for similar applications in other fields that involve continuous data analysis. The LifeStream engine can process streams of up to 100 kilobytes per second in a single node, supporting streams that are approximately four times larger than similar stream processing engines. The development of LifeStream also demonstrates the effectiveness of converting complex algorithms into incremental forms manually, leading to a 5x improvement in processing time when compared to automatically generated incremental forms. The LifeStream engine has been optimized for periodic streams and can process streams that are 3.5 times larger than batch engines like Apache Spark, while reducing memory usage to 50% of that required by these batch engines. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. Specifically, we establish and verify the characteristics of the (1,3)-Bertrand curve, and find that it can be represented by a curve of constant curvature. Furthermore, we examine and define the (1,3)-Bertrand curve in a general $n$-dimensional Euclidean space, and explore its relationship to curves of constant curvature. Additionally, we determine its Lie symmetries and classify it based on its differential invariance.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification setting. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we develop a straightforward algorithm for updating the loss function during training and evaluate it using real-world datasets, achieving performance gains of up to 6.7% in certain cases. Our work's results, coupled with its methodology, are relevant to ongoing research on dynamic loss functions and reinforcement learning-based loss optimization. Our code is available at this link: https://github.com/ghamidian/Evaluating-Loss-Functions-in-Deep-Learning.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. Computational simulations are compared to experimental data, demonstrating the model's accuracy in material modeling. The proposed model offers a valuable tool for predicting temperature changes and material microstructure evolution in polymer materials subjected to varying temperatures and mechanical loads during manufacturing, material processing, and final product design stages. The model's applicability has been demonstrated for specific thermoplastic polyurethane materials but can be extended to other polymer materials with strain-induced crystallization behavior. The model source code is available online for download. The model's limitations and potential areas for further development are also discussed. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is examined, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized solution for $K$. This solution minimizes performance loss, measured by signal-to-noise ratio erosion, to manageable levels, and facilitates seamless integration into various systems through straightforward delay-only modification. Consequently, it offers a practical degree of design-degree-of-freedom to system designers. Numerical computation and subsequent simulation validation are performed to ensure the accuracy of the proposed solution. Moreover, this research delivers a specific example of optimized differential detection for systems with time-varying channels, where the delay period remains constant as the data is transmitted. This leads to a notable improvement in system performance, as measured by bit error rate. In particular, the optimized solution for $K=4$ cuts the required $6$ dB Eb/N0 needed for coherent detection by half, to a required $3$ dB Eb/N0, when the delay period is set to two symbol durations. This indicates that, when the system is designed with sufficient margin, the performance loss is negligible, resulting in a design that is virtually indistinguishable from its coherent detection counterpart. This design can be applied to various systems, including those utilizing binary CPM, minimum shift keying, and continuous shift keying. In addition to its use in time-invariant channels, this research delivers a practical solution for systems with Doppler shift frequencies up to $f_dT_s = 0.05$, which is highly resistant to channel disturbances and provides a convenient degree of design freedom to system designers. In conclusion, this research delivers a straightforward delay-only design freedom to system designers that results in a performance gain to the conventional differential detection system. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  Each entry in ATOMIC takes the form of a statement that a particular situation (an "antecedent") leads to a specific consequence (a "consequent") in a particular way (a "inference type"). We assemble this dataset to facilitate the development of artificial intelligence models capable of basic reasoning. To demonstrate the utility of ATOMIC, we create a straightforward, result-oriented evaluation metric called "ReasonType" in addition to the commonly used "ExtraTrees" evaluation method. Both assessment approaches reveal that incorporating a set of carefully selected reasoning-type signals enhances the performance of models in a range of tasks, including selecting the most suitable conclusion when given multiple options. With its unique structure and vast quantity of data, ATOMIC also enables the development of a diverse set of models that excel in various benchmarks of commonsense reasoning, including a particular challenge that prioritizes the use of verbal descriptions. We believe that this dataset holds significant value for continued research in the field of commonsense reasoning.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in finance that involves selecting the most beneficial investment mix to achieve set risk and return parameters. Due to the intricate nature of option pricing and varying market variables, portfolio optimization must be carried out regularly to accommodate market changes. While classical computers can perform portfolio optimization efficiently, they are hindered by limitations in accessing real-time market data. Quantum computers, utilizing the HHL algorithm, can significantly speed up portfolio optimization through matrix exponential calculation and variational hybrid classical-quantum methods. However, current quantum devices are prone to errors, necessitating a hybrid approach that combines classical pre-quantum processing, real-valued portfolio optimization, and a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm tailored to the available quantum resources. We developed QHFEO, a hybrid framework that leverages the hybrid HHL (hybrid HHL) algorithm to efficiently optimize portfolios on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware by: selecting a suitable quantum register configuration, developing a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm to minimize quantum errors, and creating a portfolio optimization solution using real-valued variables. We applied QHFEO to the hybrid HHL algorithm to optimize portfolios for the COBOL-60 graph-induced Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation, utilizing a quantum device with 32 qubits and achieving a 99.7% accuracy in just 1500 hybrid iterations. We also explored the impact of the hybrid HHL algorithm's parameters on its performance and discovered that the quantum device's coherence time has a substantial impact on performance, with a 20x improvement in simulation speed achievable through proper tuning. We believe that our findings have significant implications for the practical application of quantum portfolio optimization on NISQ devices and provide actionable advice for tackling real-world portfolio optimization challenges. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models, a method has been proposed to integrate ASR models with text classification models using a multi-modal learning approach. Initially, a speech-text classification model is trained to classify speech by categorizing corresponding text. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon. The term "quantum interference" itself might be misleading as it implies a role of high-order coherent quantum phase slips which could block conduction, but our findings suggest alternative explanations such as the role of single coherent quantum phase slips or other effects that could replicate the observed patterns. The prevalence of these unusual phenomena in nanowires with varying dimensions suggests there might be a characteristic length scale unique to NbN. By combining theoretical modeling and experimental measurements, we aim to clarify the mechanisms governing these phenomena and determine the specific parameters of the nanowires studied. The unique features of our measurements also raise the possibility of utilizing superconducting nanowires as precision voltage standards based on the reproducibility of their periodic variations. For applications in video-based surveillance and virtual reality, predicting videos from novel viewpoints is a highly desirable capability. In this work, we focus on predicting videos from a front-facing perspective given rear-facing views. We introduce a dual representation framework where two separate latent variables, one for each viewpoint, encode sequential video data. During training, these variables intertwine to enable viewpoint-neutral reconstruction. In the prediction phase, we use the pre-trained encoder to generate the latent variables and decode the predicted video. Our method achieves superior results compared to baseline approaches in novel view video prediction, demonstrating the effectiveness of encoding multiple viewpoints within a single encoder. Moreover, we establish that, with sufficient data, our method can differentiate between viewpoints without prior knowledge. Our approach also extends to multi-view prediction by simply incorporating an additional latent variable. Our code will be publicly available upon publication. For novel view video prediction from a 2D perspective, our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods by a considerable margin, with over 12 psnr and 3 mse improvements for certain sequences. Our method can be trained end-to-end using a simple reconstruction loss without the need for additional supervision or view-aware data. We believe our approach has the potential to excel in a variety of novel view prediction scenarios.

We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications. Our findings also highlighted the versatility of photonic chip mode converters that can spatially position mode conversion at desired locations, anywhere within a photonic chip. Our developed device can be a critical component for future quantum computing and other interference-based photonic systems that rely on precise mode conversion and interference. Our research has been theoretically verified by numerical simulations using the beam propagation method. Our developed device has a mode conversion efficiency of over 90% and a side lobe of less than 5% and can be easily integrated with other photonic components to create a complex beam splitter or mode converter for a wide range of photonic applications. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses can be difficult to predict due to varying airflow patterns and the impact of breathing on aerosol dispersal. We used computational fluid dynamics to simulate airflow and modeled the dispersal of aerosols from a talking person within a moving bus to better understand the factors influencing the spread of airborne pathogens among passengers. We found that a simplified model assuming perfect mixing can accurately replicate the results of the more complex computational model, even when considering the effects of breathing. This finding suggests that a more straightforward model, without the need for computational fluid dynamics, can effectively estimate the risk of disease transmission among bus passengers. We also identified the key factors influencing the distribution of aerosols and the associated risk of transmission, including the speed of the bus, the distance between passengers, and the presence of recirculating air. By utilizing a simplified model, we were able to determine that a bus's length should be no more than three times its width to minimize the transmission risk. By applying these insights, we believe it's possible to develop general guidelines for reducing the transmission of airborne diseases in similar enclosed environments. We hope this study's results will be useful to bus operators, transportation authorities, and public health officials working to minimize the spread of infectious diseases in urban settings.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a strong influence of Spin-Orbit Coupling resulting from the interaction between materials with different Spin-Orbit Coupling values. We examined the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in a Bilayer made of Cobalt and Bismuth by calculating the electronic properties using the Semi-empirical Slater-Koster method. As Bismuth's strong Spin-Orbit Coupling primarily affects the $\sigma$-orbital due to its limited hybridization with Cobalt's $\sigma$-orbital, we observed a significant influence of the Spin-Orbit Coupling on the $\sigma$-orbital within the Cobalt layer near the Interface. This impact is noticeable when the thickness of the Bismuth layer is minimal and diminishes with increasing thickness as the influence of the Interface Scattering comes into play, counteracting the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect. This is further supported by calculations of the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect's dependence on the Angle of Incidence during X-ray Photoemission Spectroscopy, indicating that the Effect's reduction can be attributed to Interface Scattering rather than the Increased thickness of the Cobalt layer. This finding underlines the significance of considering Interface Scattering when studying the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in Heterostructures. This is in addition to the Influence of Spin-Orbit Coupling, Half-Filling, and Correlation. This study's approach and results also provide a framework for studying other Heterostructures made of various materials.
