We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal field, with up to 4 electrons per site in a single band, with both local and itinerant behaviors in mind. By directly comparing the mixing angles obtained through minimization of the free energy in the frameworks of Hartree-Fock and dynamical mean-field theory, we find that the spin-orbit coupling's impact on these angles is significantly reduced as compared to their magnitude, with mixings of approximately 10-20 degrees resulting due to strong electron interactions. Notably, this predicted mixing is lower than the 30-50 degrees typically assumed in past studies. Additionally, we propose a simplified expression for the mixing angles based on precise numerical data. By applying this approach to 4d and 5d transition metal oxides, we find that the proposed expression accurately captures both doped Mott insulators and correlated metals' behavior, with the mixings ranging from 10 to 30 degrees. With this analysis in hand, we hope to provide a more precise understanding of the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing essential for correctly interpreting and comparing the results of various theoretical models used to study these materials.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. Additionally, it provides formulas for the integrated rank of I-functions for certain types of toric complete intersections, which are related to specific combinations of Lie algebra weights. Furthermore, it explores how the relative I-functions behave when these types of intersections are transformed through a specific mathematical operation called toric transformations. Finally, it discusses the implications of these findings for another related mathematical system called FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical image editing is demonstrated, where a trained model can alter normal X-rays into simulated images depicting specific diseases. We utilized a pre-trained model capable of classifying 13 respiratory conditions and employed it to generate synthetic images reflecting lung cancer. By incorporating a new loss function, we successfully edited normal X-rays to resemble those with the target condition, as verified by medical professionals. Human subjects also confirmed the edited images appeared credible. The developed technique can be valuable for various purposes, including but not limited to training and evaluating deep learning models, accelerating simulation-based clinical trials, and enhancing realistic simulation for surgical planning. By combining GAN-based editing and classification techniques, we created a straightforward protocol that other researchers can build upon to explore more complex conditions affecting the lung tissue. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub at the URL mentioned herein. The generated code utilizes the PyTorch framework and consists of a U-Net architecture trained using the adversarial L1 loss technique described in the paper referenced herein. The code includes instructions for installing required software, generating fake images, and reproducing the results presented in the Figures included with this submission. The developed model achieved a generalization score of 0.45 when applied to images outside its training set, demonstrating some level of cross-validation validity. The protocol used in this research can be expanded to develop a more comprehensive respiratory disease dataset, which could be beneficial in evaluating artificial intelligence algorithms used in the diagnosis of respiratory diseases. The developed technique has limitations, as it only accurately recreated the white opacities associated with lung cancer, whereas real-world images exhibit a more varied range of tumor characteristics. The code for this research includes instructions for training the model on a single GPU within 24 hours, as well as modifying the model to create images featuring different types of tumors, metastases, and other abnormalities affecting the lung tissue. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. It is available for use on Windows systems
and can be downloaded at no cost.
